[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance helps Product Engineering teams estimate the effort required to prepare a product for extensibility under the Customer-Funded Customization strategy. It does not provide specific hour or sprint estimates — those depend entirely on product-specific variables that only the team can measure. Instead, this guidance identifies the complexity drivers that most influence effort, describes the relative effort profile of each Phase 1 activity, provides an input worksheet for capturing product-specific variables, and catalogs the scope risks that most commonly expand effort beyond initial expectations.

Used alongside [GUID-APP-IMPL-004 Product Engineering Extensibility Bootstrapping Guide](./GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md), this guidance enables a product engineering team to construct a defensible, product-specific effort estimate for roadmap planning and business case purposes.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#business-value]

### Business Value

- Enables Product Engineering leads to build credible effort estimates for extensibility roadmap investment conversations
- Surfaces scope risks before planning is committed, reducing mid-execution surprises
- Provides a common vocabulary for discussing effort complexity with Product Management and DDI leadership
- Anchors estimates to product-specific variables rather than industry averages, reducing estimation error
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#target-audience]

### Target Audience

- **Primary Audience**: Product Engineering Leads, Principal Engineers, and Architects building roadmap estimates for extensibility work
- **Secondary Audience**: Product Management and Program Management consuming estimates to plan DDI engagement timelines
- **Stakeholders**: DDI Leadership and Enterprise Architecture — for understanding why effort varies across products
page_texts.8:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#applicable-scenarios]

#### Applicable Scenarios

- **Pre-Roadmap Planning**: A product team is scoping extensibility work prior to roadmap commitment
- **Business Case Development**: Leadership requires an effort justification for extensibility investment
- **Scope Risk Assessment**: A team wants to identify and mitigate estimation risks before execution begins
- **Cross-Product Comparison**: A program office is comparing extensibility readiness and effort across multiple products
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#scope-boundaries]

#### Scope Boundaries

- **In Scope**: Effort estimation for Phase 1 extensibility work (extension point design, plugin system, SDK, testing harnesses, documentation) as defined in [GUID-APP-IMPL-004](./GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md)
- **Out of Scope**: Effort estimation for Phase 2 or Phase 3 activities (those depend on Phase 1 findings), DDI team implementation effort (DDI teams own their own estimates), and infrastructure provisioning effort (servers, environments, CI/CD pipeline setup)
- **Related Guidance**: [GUID-APP-IMPL-004: Bootstrapping Guide](./GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md), [GUID-APP-IMPL-002: Extension Pattern Cookbook](./GUID-APP-IMPL-002-extension-pattern-cookbook.md)

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#business-drivers]

#### Business Drivers

- **Roadmap Credibility**: Product Engineering cannot commit to enabling extensibility without a defensible effort estimate; without one, the work will be continuously deferred
- **DDI Dependency**: DDI teams cannot begin customer customization work until Product Engineering Phase 1 is complete — inaccurate estimates cascade directly to customer delivery commitments
- **Investment Justification**: Extensibility work competes against feature development for engineering capacity; a structured estimation approach makes the investment case explicit and comparable
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#strategic-alignment]

#### Strategic Alignment

This guidance supports the [Customer-Funded Product Customization Strategy](../../../white-papers/engineering/customer-funded-customization-strategy.md) by ensuring that Product Engineering teams can translate the strategy's implementation requirements into defensible roadmap commitments. Estimation is a prerequisite for the protected capacity allocation identified as a Critical Success Factor in [GUID-APP-IMPL-004](./GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md).
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#current-state-assessment]

#### Current State Assessment

- Products vary significantly in their readiness to receive extensibility: some have clean pipeline architectures where extension points can be wired with low disruption; others require significant internal refactoring before any extension points can be exposed
- No standard effort baseline exists across products because no product has yet completed Phase 1 implementation — estimates must be derived from product-specific analysis, not from program-level norms
- The primary source of estimation error is underestimating the effort required for extension point contract design and iteration, which depends on DDI collaboration that is difficult to schedule and compress
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#future-state-vision]

#### Future State Vision

- After the first product completes Phase 1, actual effort data will be available to calibrate future estimates using an analogy-based approach
- Over time, a program-level estimation database can be built from completed Phase 1 implementations, providing increasingly reliable baselines for similar products
page_texts.18:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#problem-description]

#### Problem Description

[GUID-APP-IMPL-004](./GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md) answers *what to build* and *in what order*, but does not help a product engineer answer *how long will this take* or *what are the main factors driving our effort*. Without structured estimation guidance, teams either produce unreliable estimates based on intuition or avoid estimating at all — both of which undermine roadmap credibility and capacity planning.
page_texts.19:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#impact-assessment]

#### Impact Assessment

- Underestimates cause mid-execution scope negotiations and missed DDI delivery windows
- Overestimates cause investment to be rejected or deferred, blocking the strategy
- Without a complexity driver framework, teams cannot explain *why* their estimate differs from another product's estimate, creating cross-team confusion in program-level planning
page_texts.20:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#success-criteria]

### Success Criteria

| Success Area | Metrics | Measurement Approach | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Estimate Defensibility | Estimate is traceable to documented product-specific inputs | Review estimate worksheet completeness | All complexity driver inputs populated before estimate is submitted |
| Scope Risk Visibility | Scope risks identified and rated before planning commitment | Count of risks with documented mitigations | All high-probability risks have mitigation strategies documented |
| Estimate Accuracy | Actual Phase 1 effort vs. estimated effort | Tracked post-completion | Defined at program outset based on acceptable variance |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#principle-1-estimate-from-product-specific-inputs-not-analogies]

#### Principle 1: Estimate from Product-Specific Inputs, Not Analogies

**Description:** Every effort estimate for extensibility work must be derived from inputs specific to the product being assessed — number of identified customization seams, codebase architecture characteristics, team experience, and existing technical debt. Generic industry benchmarks or estimates from other products are unreliable starting points because product-to-product variation in these inputs is high.

**Rationale:** The single largest driver of estimation error in extensibility work is applying estimates from one product to another without accounting for the structural differences between them. A product with a clean pipeline architecture and two identified customization seams requires fundamentally different effort than a product with event-driven orchestration and twelve customization seams embedded in legacy spaghetti code.

**Application:** Complete the Effort Input Worksheet (see Practical Application) before producing any effort estimate. The worksheet forces capture of the product-specific variables that most influence effort. No estimate should be submitted without a completed worksheet.
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#principle-2-treat-contract-design-effort-as-the-dominant-phase-1-variable]

#### Principle 2: Treat Contract Design Effort as the Dominant Phase 1 Variable

**Description:** Of all Phase 1 activities, extension point contract design — defining the interface signatures, input context types, output types, and execution model for each extension point — is consistently the most effort-intensive relative to its apparent simplicity. It requires multiple rounds of review with DDI teams and Enterprise Architecture, and each revision cycle adds elapsed time that cannot be parallelized.

**Rationale:** Contract design cannot be rushed without creating downstream rework costs. An extension point contract published to DDI teams is effectively a public API — breaking changes after publication require coordinated migration across all consuming teams. The cost of getting it wrong is asymmetrically high.

**Application:** When estimating, isolate contract design effort from implementation effort. Assume contract design will require at least two rounds of DDI review after the initial draft. Add buffer for revision cycles in your estimate; do not assume the first draft will be accepted.
page_texts.25:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#principle-3-scope-risk-is-the-largest-source-of-estimate-variance]

#### Principle 3: Scope Risk Is the Largest Source of Estimate Variance

**Description:** The difference between a well-executed Phase 1 and an over-run Phase 1 is almost always one or more scope risks materializing: discovering that the product's pipelines do not have clean seams and require refactoring before extension points can be wired; discovering that an identified customization seam traverses a legacy module that no engineer currently understands; or discovering mid-execution that the DDI partner team is unavailable for validation.

**Rationale:** Scope risks in extensibility work are largely predictable from product characteristics known before execution begins. By identifying and rating risks upfront, teams can either mitigate them (reducing the likelihood they materialize) or carry explicit contingency in the estimate (acknowledging the risk rather than hiding it).

**Application:** Complete the Scope Risk Catalog (see Practical Application) before finalizing any estimate. Risks rated as High probability must have documented mitigation strategies. The estimate should include explicit contingency for unmitigated High risks.
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#principle-4-relative-effort-ordering-is-more-reliable-than-absolute-estimates]

#### Principle 4: Relative Effort Ordering Is More Reliable Than Absolute Estimates

**Description:** When communicating effort across activities, use relative sizing (highest effort / moderate effort / lower effort) before committing to absolute estimates. Relative sizing captures the team's confidence in effort ordering — which activities dominate — without false precision in absolute numbers.

**Rationale:** Absolute estimates for new work types are systematically under-precise because there is no comparable prior work to anchor them. Relative sizing is more honest about uncertainty and more useful for prioritization decisions.

**Application:** Use the Phase 1 Activity Effort Profile table (see below) as the starting point for relative sizing. Adjust the relative ordering based on product-specific complexity drivers before deriving absolute estimates.
page_texts.28:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#approach-1-bottom-up-activity-level-estimation]

#### Approach 1: Bottom-Up Activity-Level Estimation

**Overview:** Estimate effort for each Phase 1 activity individually, using the complexity drivers specific to that activity, then sum to a Phase 1 total.

**When to Use:** When the team has the time and access to product source code needed to assess each activity's complexity drivers independently. Produces the most reliable estimates.

**Implementation:**
1. Enumerate Phase 1 activities from [GUID-APP-IMPL-004](./GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md)
2. For each activity, identify the applicable complexity drivers from the Complexity Driver Catalog
3. Rate each driver (high / medium / low) based on product-specific assessment
4. Derive a relative effort tier for each activity
5. Assign absolute estimates to each activity using team velocity and the relative tiers
6. Sum activities; apply scope risk contingency; present as an estimate range

**Benefits:** Traceable to specific product characteristics; reveals which activities dominate; makes scope risk visible

**Considerations:** Requires upfront access to product codebase and DDI team input; takes more time than top-down estimation
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#approach-2-top-down-profile-based-estimation]

#### Approach 2: Top-Down Profile-Based Estimation

**Overview:** Classify the product into an overall effort profile (Low / Moderate / High complexity) based on the dominant complexity drivers, then apply a relative multiplier from a baseline estimate anchored to the pilot product's actuals.

**When to Use:** When speed of estimate is required for early planning conversations, or when a comparable prior implementation exists to anchor the baseline. Note: prior to any completed Phase 1, a true anchor baseline does not exist — treat any top-down estimate as provisional.

**Implementation:**
1. Complete the [Effort Input Worksheet](#template-1-effort-input-worksheet) (abbreviated — focus on the top five complexity drivers)
2. Classify each driver as Low / Moderate / High
3. Determine the overall product complexity profile from the majority classification
4. Apply a relative multiplier to any available baseline estimate (e.g., pilot product actuals)
5. Present as a range with explicit acknowledgment that the baseline is provisional

**Benefits:** Fast; useful for early-stage planning conversations

**Considerations:** Requires a completed anchor baseline to be reliable; without one, it is essentially intuition structured into a framework
page_texts.31:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#best-practice-1-separate-elapsed-time-from-effort]

#### Best Practice 1: Separate Elapsed Time from Effort

**Description:** Clearly distinguish between total engineering effort (e.g., person-days of work) and elapsed calendar time in any estimate. The two diverge significantly in extensibility work because contract design and DDI review iterations introduce waiting time that cannot be eliminated by adding more engineers.

**Rationale:** Stakeholders often conflate effort and elapsed time. Presenting only one creates mismatched expectations — a low effort estimate with high elapsed time due to review cycles will appear to stakeholders as a slow-moving team.

**Implementation:** Present estimates in two dimensions: (1) engineering effort in person-days or sprint points, and (2) elapsed time in sprints or calendar periods reflecting estimated review cycle wait times.

**Success Indicators:** Stakeholders understand and accept that calendar time includes non-engineering wait periods; review cycle buffer is explicitly visible in the schedule.
page_texts.32:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#best-practice-2-version-your-estimate-as-inputs-change]

#### Best Practice 2: Version Your Estimate as Inputs Change

**Description:** As the team learns more during preparation (completing the customization inventory, reviewing the codebase, engaging with the DDI partner team), update the estimate and record what changed and why. Treat estimation as an iterative process, not a one-time event.

**Rationale:** Estimates produced before the customization inventory is complete are necessarily less reliable than estimates produced after. Documenting how estimates change as inputs are refined builds stakeholder confidence and creates an audit trail.

**Implementation:** Use the Estimate Version Log template (see Templates and Artifacts) to record estimate versions, the inputs that changed, and the resulting estimate adjustment.

**Success Indicators:** Estimate versions are traceable to specific new information; stakeholders can see estimate confidence increasing as preparation activities complete.
page_texts.33:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#best-practice-3-gate-estimate-submission-on-customization-inventory-completion]

#### Best Practice 3: Gate Estimate Submission on Customization Inventory Completion

**Description:** Do not submit a Phase 1 effort estimate to stakeholders before the customization inventory is complete. The inventory is the primary input to the most important complexity driver (count and complexity of customization seams), and without it, estimates are unreliable.

**Rationale:** The customization inventory takes time but is short relative to Phase 1 execution. Submitting an estimate before it is complete introduces predictable error that will require a reforecast early in Phase 1 — undermining credibility at the worst time.

**Implementation:** Include customization inventory completion as a prerequisite for final estimate submission in the team's planning process. Provide a preliminary range estimate before inventory, with explicit notation that it will be revised after inventory completion.

**Success Indicators:** Final estimate submission is accompanied by a completed customization inventory; preliminary and final estimate ranges are clearly labeled as such.
page_texts.35:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#pitfall-1-estimating-implementation-without-estimating-contract-design]

#### Pitfall 1: Estimating Implementation Without Estimating Contract Design

**Description:** Teams estimate the coding effort for plugin system, SDK, and testing harnesses but treat extension point contract design as a non-effort administrative task. This systematically underestimates Phase 1 because contract design is the highest-effort activity.

**Impact:** Estimates may be materially too low; Phase 1 will appear to be running over-budget from the first sprint because contract design consumes far more time than estimated.

**Prevention:** Explicitly include contract design effort as a line item in every Phase 1 estimate. Include DDI review cycle wait times as elapsed-time buffer.

**Mitigation:** If this has already occurred, reforecast immediately with a corrected contract design estimate rather than absorbing the variance silently.
page_texts.36:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#pitfall-2-assuming-existing-pipelines-have-clean-extension-seams]

#### Pitfall 2: Assuming Existing Pipelines Have Clean Extension Seams

**Description:** Teams estimate based on the assumption that extension points can be wired into existing pipelines with minor code changes. In many products, the pipelines have state-specific logic deeply embedded, and exposing a clean extension seam requires significant refactoring first.

**Impact:** Discovering mid-execution that a pipeline requires refactoring before an extension point can be wired is one of the most common causes of Phase 1 scope expansion.

**Prevention:** During the customization inventory, explicitly evaluate each identified seam for pipeline cleanliness. Assess whether the seam currently has clean separation between core logic and customer-specific logic, or whether refactoring is required first.

**Mitigation:** If discovered mid-execution, scope the refactoring explicitly, communicate the updated estimate, and prioritize the cleanest seam over the highest-priority seam if the two conflict.
page_texts.37:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#pitfall-3-treating-ddi-team-availability-as-certain]

#### Pitfall 3: Treating DDI Team Availability as Certain

**Description:** Contract design review and DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint both depend on DDI team availability — something Product Engineering does not control. Estimates that assume DDI availability will occur when needed are systematically optimistic.

**Impact:** DDI scheduling delays introduce waiting time that extends elapsed calendar time without consuming engineering effort, causing the project to appear behind schedule.

**Prevention:** Confirm DDI partner team availability and capacity at the start of planning, not mid-execution. Build explicit scheduling assumptions into the estimate and document them.

**Mitigation:** If DDI availability is delayed, advance other parallelizable activities (SDK build, testing harness development) to use the wait time productively.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#methodology-overview]

#### Methodology Overview

Effort estimation for extensibility work follows a three-step process: (1) Collect product-specific inputs using the Effort Input Worksheet; (2) Assess complexity and scope risk using the Complexity Driver Catalog and Scope Risk Catalog; (3) Derive and document an effort estimate using the Activity Effort Profile. Each step builds on the previous, and the estimate is progressively refined as inputs are confirmed.

| Phase 3: Estimate Derivation | Convert complexity assessment into a documented effort estimate | Apply Activity Effort Profile, derive effort range, add contingency | Versioned estimate document with input traceability |

page_texts.47:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#phase-1-input-collection]

#### Phase 1: Input Collection

**Objectives:** Capture the product-specific inputs that drive effort estimation with sufficient fidelity to support complexity rating

**Key Activities:**
1. **Complete the Customization Inventory** — enumerate all locations in the product codebase where customer/state-specific logic currently exists; record location, workflow area, estimated line count, and whether the seam appears clean or embedded
2. **Conduct Pipeline Architecture Review** — for each identified seam, assess pipeline architecture: is the extension point hookable with minor wiring, or does it require refactoring to expose a clean seam?
3. **Assess Team Capability** — rate the team's prior experience with .NET extensibility patterns, NuGet package publishing, and test harness development; identify gaps that add learning curve to the estimate
4. **Confirm DDI Partner Availability** — confirm when the DDI partner team can participate in contract design review and the DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint

**Deliverables:** Completed [Effort Input Worksheet](#template-1-effort-input-worksheet) with all fields populated
page_texts.48:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#phase-2-complexity-assessment]

#### Phase 2: Complexity Assessment

**Objectives:** Convert the raw inputs into structured complexity ratings for each driver and risk

**Key Activities:**
1. **Complete the Complexity Driver Catalog** — for each driver, assign a Low / Moderate / High rating based on the Effort Input Worksheet data
2. **Determine Overall Activity Effort Tiers** — using the Activity Effort Profile, adjust relative effort tiers for each Phase 1 activity based on complexity driver ratings
3. **Complete the Scope Risk Catalog** — rate the probability and impact of each scope risk; document mitigation strategies for High-probability risks

**Deliverables:** Rated Complexity Driver Catalog, Rated Scope Risk Catalog with mitigations
page_texts.49:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#phase-3-estimate-derivation]

#### Phase 3: Estimate Derivation

**Objectives:** Produce a versioned, traceable effort estimate with explicit contingency for unmitigated risks

**Key Activities:**
1. **Apply Activity Effort Profile** — assign absolute effort estimates to each activity using team velocity and the complexity-adjusted relative tiers
2. **Sum to Phase 1 Total** — compute total engineering effort; separate into parallel vs. sequential activities to derive elapsed calendar time
3. **Add Scope Risk Contingency** — for each unmitigated High-probability risk, add explicit contingency to the effort total; document the contingency separately from the base estimate
4. **Version and Publish** — record the estimate version, input assumptions, and contingency rationale in the Estimate Version Log

**Deliverables:** Versioned effort estimate with activity-level breakdown, effort vs. elapsed time presentation, and explicit risk contingency
page_texts.51:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#critical-success-factor-1-customization-inventory-quality]

#### Critical Success Factor 1: Customization Inventory Quality

**Description:** The customization inventory is the foundational input to the estimation process. An incomplete or superficial inventory produces an unreliable estimate.

**Importance:** The count and complexity of customization seams is the single highest-impact complexity driver. An undercount systematically produces a low estimate; an overcount wastes engineering effort in Phase 1.

**Implementation:** Allocate dedicated capacity to completing a thorough inventory before producing the estimate. Use automated tooling (e.g., grep patterns for state-identifier conditionals, customer-id branches) to supplement manual review.

**Measurement:** Track inventory coverage: what percentage of the product's codebase and business workflows has been reviewed for customization seams.
page_texts.52:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#critical-success-factor-2-explicit-scope-risk-documentation]

#### Critical Success Factor 2: Explicit Scope Risk Documentation

**Description:** Every estimate must be accompanied by a completed Scope Risk Catalog. Estimates submitted without explicit risk documentation are incomplete and should be rejected by reviewers.

**Importance:** Scope risk is the largest driver of actual vs. estimated variance. Making risks explicit enables stakeholders to make informed decisions about risk acceptance vs. mitigation investment.

**Implementation:** Use the Scope Risk Catalog template (see Templates and Artifacts) for every estimate. Present risks alongside the estimate, not as a footnote.

**Measurement:** Count of risks documented, count with mitigation strategies, and count accepted as contingency — all should be visible in the estimate package.

#### Preparation Steps

1. **Gather Estimation Inputs**
   - Required inputs: Product source code access, existing DDI change request history, team roster with relevant skill experience, DDI partner team contact and availability calendar
   - Key activities: Schedule customization inventory work session; schedule pipeline architecture review with a senior product engineer; schedule DDI partner availability confirmation call
   - Expected output: Populated Effort Input Worksheet (all fields)

2. **Read Phase 1 Activities**
   - Familiarize with the Phase 1 activity sequence in [GUID-APP-IMPL-004](./GUID-APP-IMPL-004-product-engineering-extensibility-bootstrapping-guidance.md) before beginning complexity assessment — estimating requires understanding what is being estimated
   - Pay particular attention to the dependency annotations (e.g., "depends on: Extension Point Catalog approved") as these determine which activities are sequential vs. parallel, directly affecting elapsed time
page_texts.56:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#execution-steps]

#### Execution Steps

1. **Complete the [Effort Input Worksheet](#template-1-effort-input-worksheet)**
   - Work through all fields; do not skip fields on the assumption they are not relevant — missing fields are a common source of underestimation

2. **Rate Each Complexity Driver**

   | Complexity Driver | Drives Effort For | Low | Moderate | High |
   |---|---|---|---|---|
   | Number of identified customization seams | Extension point design, plugin wiring | ≤ 3 seams | 4–7 seams | 8+ seams |
   | Pipeline cleanliness at seam locations | Plugin wiring, refactoring pre-work | All seams hookable with minor wiring | 1–2 seams require focused refactoring | Multiple seams require significant refactoring |
   | Greenfield vs. retrofit | Extension point design, pipeline wiring | Greenfield — no existing ad-hoc customizations | Retrofit — limited ad-hoc customization | Retrofit — extensive or deeply embedded ad-hoc customization |
   | Team's prior .NET extensibility experience | SDK build, plugin system | Team has prior experience with plugin patterns and NuGet publishing | Mixed experience | No team member has extensibility framework experience |
   | Frontend extension scope | All frontend activities | No frontend customization required (defer frontend to Phase 2) | Frontend in scope, modern React stack | Frontend in scope, legacy or mixed stack |
   | DDI partner availability | Contract design review cycles, validation sprint | Confirmed availability aligned to schedule | Partial availability; some scheduling risk | Unconfirmed; high scheduling risk |
   | Existing test coverage in pipeline areas being wired | Compatibility harness build, regression risk | Strong test coverage at seam locations | Moderate test coverage | Sparse or no test coverage; harness must be built before wiring begins |
   | Multi-tenant isolation testing | Isolation test harness, Phase 2 readiness | Product is single-tenant; isolation harness scope is minimal | Product has limited multi-tenant deployment; isolation scope is bounded | Product is fully multi-tenant; isolation harness is a HIPAA compliance control and cannot be excluded or deferred |

3. **Apply the Activity Effort Profile**

   Use the following relative effort profile as the default ordering for Phase 1, then adjust tiers based on your complexity driver ratings:

   | Phase 1 Activity | Default Relative Effort | Primary Complexity Drivers |
   |---|---|---|
   | Extension point contract design + DDI review cycles | Highest | Number of seams, DDI availability |
   | Extension framework security architecture (threat model, FIPS 199, control selection) | High | Greenfield vs. retrofit, multi-tenant isolation testing |
   | Plugin system implementation + pipeline wiring (including load-time signature verification) | High | Pipeline cleanliness, test coverage at seams, number of seams |
   | SDK core package (base classes, helpers, DI wrappers, SBOM generation) | Moderate | Team .NET extensibility experience |
   | Compatibility + isolation test harnesses | Moderate | Existing test coverage, number of extension points, multi-tenant isolation testing |
   | Security testing (SAST + dependency vulnerability scanning) | Moderate | Existing test coverage, greenfield vs. retrofit |
   | `dotnet new` templates + Extension Contracts package (signed, strong-named) | Lower | Team NuGet publishing experience |
   | Documentation + sample extensions (including secrets management guidance) | Lower | Number of extension points, SDK API surface area |
   | DDI Onboarding Validation Sprint | Lower (elapsed time–intensive, low engineering effort) | DDI availability, documentation completeness |

4. **Complete the Scope Risk Catalog and Document Contingency**

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#decision-point-1-bottom-up-vs-top-down-estimation]

#### Decision Point 1: Bottom-Up vs. Top-Down Estimation

**Context:** The team must choose between a thorough bottom-up estimate (requires completing the customization inventory first) and a faster top-down profile estimate (useful for early planning, but less reliable).

**Options:** (A) Complete customization inventory first, then produce bottom-up estimate; (B) Produce a top-down profile estimate now, commit to refining after inventory

**Criteria:** How soon a committed estimate is needed; whether a comparable prior implementation exists to anchor a top-down estimate; stakeholder tolerance for a wide estimate range

**Recommendation:** Default to Option B (preliminary range now, refined estimate after inventory) if a committed estimate is needed before inventory can complete. Be explicit with stakeholders that the preliminary range carries a wide variance and will be revised.
page_texts.60:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#decision-point-2-how-to-handle-high-probability-scope-risks]

#### Decision Point 2: How to Handle High-Probability Scope Risks

**Context:** One or more scope risks are rated High probability. The team must decide whether to invest in mitigation now (reducing the risk and the base estimate) or to carry the risk as explicit contingency.

**Options:** (A) Invest in mitigation upfront (e.g., perform pipeline refactoring before Phase 1 begins); (B) Accept the risk and add explicit contingency to the estimate; (C) Descope the affected seam to Phase 2 to reduce Phase 1 risk

**Criteria:** Cost of mitigation vs. cost of contingency; whether the affected seam is a high-priority DDI requirement; timeline pressure

**Recommendation:** For risks related to pipeline cleanliness, Option A (refactoring upfront) is frequently the most cost-effective approach. Attempting to wire extension points into an unclean pipeline mid-Phase 1 is more disruptive than refactoring before starting.

page_texts.63:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#techniques-and-methods]

#### Techniques and Methods

- **Planning Poker for Activity-Level Estimates**: Once complexity drivers are rated, use planning poker with the engineering team to assign relative story points to each activity before converting to absolute estimates — leverages collective team knowledge before committing to numbers
- **Three-Point Estimation**: For activities with high uncertainty (particularly contract design and pipeline wiring), use three-point estimation (optimistic / most likely / pessimistic) and present as a range rather than a single number
- **Reference Class Forecasting**: After the first product completes Phase 1, build an actual effort reference class. Future estimates should compare the new product's complexity driver profile to the reference class product and adjust proportionally.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#use-case-1-greenfield-product--no-prior-customization]

#### Use Case 1: Greenfield Product — No Prior Customization

**Scenario Description:** A recently launched product has no existing state-specific customizations. The team needs to design extension points to support upcoming DDI engagements.

**Context:** Clean codebase, modern .NET 8 pipeline architecture, no legacy ad-hoc customization branches, small team with limited prior extensibility experience

**Complexity Driver Profile:**
- Number of seams: Low (estimated 2–3 from known DDI requirements)
- Pipeline cleanliness: Low complexity (clean architecture, hookable with minor wiring)
- Greenfield vs. retrofit: Greenfield
- Team experience: Moderate complexity (limited prior extensibility experience is a risk)
- DDI availability: Confirmed

**Guidance Application:** The dominant effort driver for this product is team learning curve on extensibility patterns and NuGet publishing, not codebase complexity. Invest in team ramp-up. Contract design effort is still the highest relative activity, but pipeline wiring efforts will be lower than a typical retrofit.

**Adaptations:** Consider adding a team enablement session (reading PTN-APP-EXT-001 through PTN-APP-EXT-005) as a preparation activity before Phase 1 begins; this reduces learning curve effort during execution.
page_texts.71:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#use-case-2-legacy-retrofit-product--extensive-prior-customization]

#### Use Case 2: Legacy Retrofit Product — Extensive Prior Customization

**Scenario Description:** A mature product has accumulated state-specific customizations across multiple workflow areas over several years of DDI engagements.

**Context:** Older .NET 6 pipeline with inconsistent architecture, ad-hoc customizations as conditional code branches, partial test coverage, active DDI teams dependent on the product

**Complexity Driver Profile:**
- Number of seams: High (inventory reveals 10+ locations)
- Pipeline cleanliness: High complexity (multiple seams require refactoring before wiring)
- Greenfield vs. retrofit: Retrofit — extensive
- Team experience: Moderate
- DDI availability: Risk — multiple active engagements competing for DDI team time

**Guidance Application:** This product has two dominant complexity drivers: pipeline cleanliness and DDI availability. Mitigation recommendations: (1) Phase the refactoring — address the highest-density seams first and accept them as Phase 1; defer lower-priority seams to Phase 2; (2) Establish a DDI review schedule 4–6 weeks before it is needed; do not assume ad-hoc availability. The Phase 1 estimate for this product will be materially higher than the greenfield scenario above.

**Adaptations:** Recommend splitting the estimate into two components: (a) core Phase 1 effort for the highest-priority 3–4 seams, and (b) refactoring pre-work effort for the pipeline areas that are not cleanly hookable. Present these separately so stakeholders understand the investment breakdown.
page_texts.73:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#implementation-lessons]

#### Implementation Lessons

- **The customization inventory always reveals more seams than initial estimates assume**: Teams that rely on DDI memory of where customizations exist consistently undercount relative to a code-level inventory. Always do a code-level review.
- **Contract design review cycles vary significantly by DDI team engagement style**: Some DDI teams have strong opinions on interface design and require multiple revision cycles; others accept the first draft. This is not predictable until the first DDI review session occurs. Budget for revision cycles.
- **Elapsed time for contract review cannot be compressed by assigning more engineers**: It is a scheduling bottleneck, not a resource bottleneck. More engineers on the SDK build does not shorten the contract review wait.
page_texts.74:
[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#best-practices-discovered]

#### Best Practices Discovered

- **Present estimates as ranges, not point estimates**: Range estimates communicate inherent uncertainty honestly and reduce stakeholder expectation misalignment when actual effort falls within the range.
- **Attach the Complexity Driver Catalog rating to every estimate**: Estimates without their input rationale are questioned; estimates with documented reasoning are defended more easily.
- **Track actual effort per activity during Phase 1 execution**: The data from the first completed Phase 1 is the most valuable estimation asset the program will have for all future products.

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#governance-structure]

#### Governance Structure

- **Estimate Review Gate**: Phase 1 effort estimates must be reviewed by Enterprise Architecture before submission to Product Management for roadmap planning — this ensures the estimate has been assessed for completeness and risk documentation
- **Reforecast Trigger Policy**: If actual Phase 1 effort variance from estimate exceeds a threshold agreed at program outset, a formal reforecast is required rather than silent absorption — the threshold should be established with Product Management before Phase 1 begins
- **Actuals Capture Requirement**: After Phase 1 completion, the product team is expected to record actual effort per activity and submit to the program estimation database to improve future estimates

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#risk-assessment]

#### Risk Assessment

| Risk Category | Risk Description | Probability | Impact | Mitigation Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory Undercount | Customization seams are undercounted due to incomplete inventory | Moderate | High | Require code-level inventory, not memory-based; supplement with automated search tooling |
| Pipeline Cleanliness Discovery | Extension seams require refactoring that was not identified in pre-estimation assessment | Moderate | High | Conduct pipeline architecture review before estimate submission, not during execution |
| DDI Availability | DDI partner team unavailable when needed for review or validation | High | Moderate | Confirm DDI availability and calendar-block review sessions before estimate is submitted |
| Team Experience Gap | Team learning curve on extensibility patterns is higher than rated | Low–Moderate | Moderate | Include team enablement activities as preparation work in the estimate; do not embed learning curve in activity estimates |
| Scope Creep from DDI Requests | DDI team requests additional extension points during Phase 1 beyond those planned | Moderate | Moderate | Establish Phase 1 scope formally with DDI team before execution; changes require explicit scope change process |

[strategy/guidance/application/implementation/GUID-APP-IMPL-005-product-engineering-extensibility-effort-estimation-guidance.md#maturity-model]

### Maturity Model

| Maturity Level | Description | Characteristics | Next Steps |
|---|---|---|---|
| Level 1: Intuition-Based | Estimates based on experience and intuition | No structured input capture; no documented complexity drivers | Begin using Effort Input Worksheet |
| Level 2: Input-Driven | Estimates based on documented product-specific inputs | Effort Input Worksheet completed; complexity drivers rated | Add Scope Risk Catalog to estimate package |
| Level 3: Risk-Aware | Estimates include explicit scope risk documentation and contingency | Complexity drivers rated; Scope Risk Catalog complete; contingency itemized | Track actuals per activity during Phase 1 |
| Level 4: Calibrated | Estimates calibrated against actual Phase 1 completion data | Prior actuals available; estimates reference comparable prior implementations | Build program-level estimation database |
| Level 5: Reference-Class | All estimates anchored to a program reference class | Multiple completed Phase 1 actuals; estimation database in use; estimation variance consistently within accepted range | Continuous calibration and model refinement |
